newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel blames German SPD for blocking tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Waigel blames German SPD for blocking tax reform.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday blamed the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) for blocking government plans to slash income and corporate taxes.
"This sets us back in competition (with other countries), it damages us and the SPD must be held responsible for that," Waigel told German Radio.

A cross-party working group all but abandoned its bid to reach compromise on tax reforms on Tuesday, opening the way for government and opposition to fight out the issue in an epic campaign ahead of general elections next year.
"(SPD leader Oskar) Lafontaine thinks that he can make an election campaign out of exploiting people's frustration."
"He will fail with this strategy because you cannot make any economic and finance policy out of this (blockade) strategy," Waigel said.
But SPD chief whip Peter Struck said the party could not agree to the government plans because they would benefit businesses and the rich at the expense of ordinary workers.

"It is always better that nothing happens than that something really bad happens," Struck told Berlin's InfoRadio. "If I have stopped such injustice, then I think that I have done something right for the people of Germany."
Waigel said he would not give in over his plans and said he was "full of fighting spirit". "We are not resigned. We will go into parliament next week on the offensive," he said.

Parliament's mediation committee was due to meet on Wednesday to discuss the plans but the SPD majority on the committee was expected to vote to reject them after both sides failed to reach agreement at two days of informal negotiations.
The SPD dominated Bundesrat upper house voted down Waigel's tax reforms earlier this month.

Negotiators still held out hope that the committee could agree to scrap a capital trading tax -- which firms must pay even when they make a loss, and which would have to be introduced in eastern Germany if no deal is reached to abolish it.

But SPD proposals to cut occupational insurance charges -- and thus reduce the cost of employing workers -- are likely to fail because the government objects to how the SPD wants to finance the reduction.

Kohl's government had billed Waigel's plan to cut some 30 billion marks ($16.3 billion) in taxes as the 'reform of the century' which would boost investment and job creation in a country where unemployment is near post-war highs.
Key elements included slashing the main rate of corporation tax to 35 percent from 47 percent by 1999 and cutting the top rate of income tax to 39 percent from 53 percent.

Rejection of the tax reforms by the mediation committee will send the measures back to the Bundestag lower house of parliament, which will interrupt its summer recess to meet next Tuesday to debate the tax reforms.
There, the two sides are likely to trade the blame for the breakdown in Germany's consensus-based politics, opening the way for a marathon campaign ahead of general elections in September 1998.
